adrs.title: SMART Handler — Python vs. C
adrs.context: The CAFS SMART system requires periodic analysis of drive health counters to provide health scores, trend detection, and recommendations to the Allocator. The analysis involves mathematical computations (error ratios, variance, trend detection) that are not time-critical. Two implementation paths were considered: (1) Pure C: all logic in C, integrated directly into the mntproc. (2) Python: logic in a Python script called by the mntproc.
adrs.decision: The SMART Handler will be implemented in Python and called by the C mntproc via stdin/stdout pipes.
rationale: Iteration speed: Python allows rapid experimentation with health formulas without recompiling the entire filesystem.
Reduced complexity: the C code remains focused on I/O, locking, and crash-safe flush coordination.
Development velocity: Python's native JSON support, math libraries, and debugging tools reduce development overhead.
Separation of concerns: C owns the critical path (I/O, locking, persistence). Python owns analytics.
consequences: Positive: faster development cycle; C code stays lean.
Negative: Python interpreter adds ~15MB to binary size (acceptable).
Negative: Python call adds process spawn overhead (every 60 seconds — acceptable).
Mitigation: embedded Python interpreter is optional at compile time (--exclude=pyi).

adrs.title: SMART Flush — Crash-Safe Order
adrs.context: SMART counters are updated on every I/O. They must be persisted to disk in a crash-safe manner to avoid losing health data during power failure. The flush path must guarantee that: no data is lost beyond the flush window; the system can recover on mount; the WAL provides atomicity.
adrs.decision:
Flush order: V-SMART -> Cache SMART -> B-SMART -> WAL -> M-SMART.
1. Lock V-SMART (RAM)
2. Read diffs
3. Clear V-SMART
4. Unlock V-SMART
5. Build ANCHOR_DIFF WAL entry
6. Write Cache SMART -> fsync()
7. Write B-SMART -> fsync()
8. Append WAL entry -> fsync()
9. Mark WAL entry as committed
rationale: WAL is the source of truth: M-SMART is updated via WAL replay, guaranteeing atomicity.
Redundancy: B-SMART provides a backup if M-SMART is corrupt.
Recovery: on mount, the system checks M-SMART -> B-SMART -> Cache SMART -> WAL.
consequences: Positive: crash-safe; mount recovery is deterministic.
Positive: no data loss beyond the 60-second flush window.
Negative: extra write to Cache SMART adds overhead (but flush runs every 60 seconds).
Mitigation: flush threshold (1024 updates) triggers early flush under heavy load.

adrs.title: SMART Bucket System — Sufficient Statistics
adrs.context: To detect trends (degrading vs. stable health), the system needs historical context. Storing every SMART sample is infeasible (too much data). A simple average loses variance, min, max, and distribution information. A method was needed to compress historical data without losing mathematical accuracy for aggregate statistics.
adrs.decision: Store buckets using sufficient statistics: (count, sum, sum_sq, min, max) for each health-relevant metric. Each bucket represents a time window (default: 1 hour). The system maintains up to 24 buckets (23 full + 1 partial), giving 24 hours of history.
rationale: Mathematical accuracy: average, variance, min, max can be perfectly reconstructed across any number of buckets.
Compression: 24 buckets x ~7 metrics x 5 stats = ~2KB of memory.
No data loss for aggregation: combining buckets is a simple sum of counts, sums, sum_sq, min, max.
consequences: Positive: low memory footprint (~2KB for 24 buckets).
Positive: variance and trend detection are possible.
Negative: loss of point-in-time auditing (can't ask "what was the exact value at 2:15 AM?").
Mitigation: point-in-time auditing is not required for CAFS's health monitoring.

adrs.title: Python Integration — Embedded Interpreter
adrs.context: The SMART Handler is implemented in Python. The system must support Python execution on all target platforms (Linux x86_64, Linux i686, Windows x86_64, Windows i686) without requiring the user to install Python. Two approaches were considered: (1) System Python: rely on python3 being installed on the system. (2) Embedded Python: bundle the Python interpreter into the CAFS binary.
adrs.decision: Embed Python interpreter into the CAFS binary. Provide a compile-time option (--exclude=pyi) to use system Python instead.
rationale: No external dependencies: user doesn't need to install Python.
Works out-of-the-box: all platforms supported.
Optional fallback: --exclude=pyi allows system Python for users who want smaller binaries.
consequences: Positive: no Python installation required.
Positive: cross-platform compatibility guaranteed.
Negative: binary size increases by ~15MB (acceptable).
Mitigation: --exclude=pyi flag reduces binary size to ~2MB for users who don't need Python.

adrs.title: SMART Tables — Hierarchy and Redundancy
adrs.context: SMART counters are written by the I/O Engine on every I/O. They must be stored persistently, with redundancy and crash recovery.
adrs.decision: Four SMART tables in a hierarchy: V-SMART (RAM, volatile — I/O Engine increments on every I/O), Cache SMART (on-disk staging — batch accumulation before final flush), B-SMART (on-disk backup — redundant copy at end of drive), M-SMART (on-disk main — authoritative source of truth).
rationale: Redundancy: B-SMART provides fallback if M-SMART is corrupt.
Crash recovery: recovery checks M -> B -> Cache -> WAL.
Performance: V-SMART is RAM-based for fast I/O increments.
Batch efficiency: Cache SMART allows batch accumulation before flushing to B-SMART/M-SMART.
consequences: Positive: crash-safe; redundancy prevents data loss.
Positive: performance (V-SMART is RAM-based).
Negative: four tables increase complexity.
Mitigation: the hierarchy is well-defined and documented in fs.info.

adrs.title: I/O Engine — Anchor Redundancy Scope (Superblock + SMART Only)
adrs.context: fs.info's original anchor design (Sec.12) mirrors all six LBA0-5 pointer blocks at the end of the device, giving every anchor real structure — Superblock, Config Snapshot, Parity Block, Meta/User Pointer Table, Function Table — a distinct backup copy. Every anchor write potentially touches five backup structures in addition to the primary, and keeping them in sync adds torn-write surface without a correspondingly large safety gain: most of those structures are either reconstructable another way (Config Snapshot, via Parity XOR against Superblock) or hold pointers/metadata whose loss doesn't prevent mounting (Function Table, Meta/User Table).
adrs.decision: End-of-device redundancy is kept only for the Superblock and the SMART tables (M-SMART/B-SMART). Config Snapshot, Parity Block, Function Table, and Meta/User Pointer Table have exactly one on-disk copy each — no distinct backup content, no end-of-device mirror of their own bytes. The end-of-device anchor region (LBA0-5 mirrored) still exists as a structural pointer-recovery mechanism: LBA0 and LBA3 at the tail point back to the same single Superblock and same single Meta/User Table as the head copies; only Superblock (LBA0) is cross-linked with a genuine second copy (Superblock Backup), reachable identically from either end. LBA1/2/4 fallback pointer fields are unused — there is no second copy for them to reference.
rationale: Write amplification: every anchor update under the full-mirror design touched up to 6 structures; under this design, at most 2 (Superblock + its backup).
Torn-write surface: fewer structures to keep synchronized means fewer partial-update states a crash can leave behind.

Selective value: Config Snapshot stays indirectly recoverable via Parity XOR Superblock even with no direct backup. Function Table and Meta/User Table hold pointers/metadata, not data the filesystem can't function without — losing either costs discoverability (WAL, SMART, Zone Table locations), not the ability to mount.

Superblock and SMART are different: Superblock gates every mount (nothing proceeds without it); SMART is the ongoing health signal the Allocator consumes continuously. Both justify the redundancy cost the others don't.
consequences: Positive: significantly less write amplification per anchor update; smaller crash-window.
Positive: matches what's implemented in the I/O Engine V1 today, exactly (check() only ever repairs Superblock; there's no "Backup Parity Block" concept in the codebase).
Negative: Function Table and Meta/User Table now have zero redundancy — a checksum failure on either is unrecoverable data loss for that structure specifically.

Mitigation: consistent with the project's existing "won't die easily" floor — the filesystem stays mountable and metadata-consistent even when some data is unrecoverable; this just extends that floor to two more structures that were never load-bearing for mount itself.

Amendment (2026-09-06): fs.info Sec.12/Sec.17b, which described distinct Config Snapshot Backup / Meta-User Table Backup / Function Table Backup / Backup Parity Block structures, contradicted this ADR and were never authoritative. Corrected: the end-of-device anchor mirror is a pointer-recovery structure only, not a second copy of the real structures it points to (except Superblock, per the cross-linking above).

adrs.title: I/O Engine — V1 Scope: Superblock-Only Verification and Repair
adrs.context: The full mount pipeline (mount -> check -> remount -> confirm) needs to exist before any of it can be tested against real hardware or even a real image file. Building complete verification and auto-repair logic for every anchor structure (Config Snapshot, Parity, Function Table) before a single read/write path has been proven working risks a large amount of untested code accumulating at once.
adrs.decision: For V1, check() verifies and — when foreseeable and safe (mount is writable, a valid backup exists) — repairs only the Superblock. Config Snapshot, Parity Block, and Function Table are read at mount time but their checksums are neither verified nor acted on.
rationale: Proof of concept first: get mount/check/remount/confirm and raw read/write working end to end against a real image before adding verification breadth.

Superblock is the one structure that's load-bearing for every other step: function_table_anchor_lba, checksum algorithm IDs, and config discovery all originate from it. Nothing else in the pipeline can proceed meaningfully if it's wrong.
The other three don't gate anything yet: Config Snapshot parsing, Parity reconstruction, and Function Table's WAL/SMART pointers aren't consumed by any code path this version actually exercises.
consequences: Positive: a small, fully tested, fully working core (24/24 assertions passing against mkfs_cafs-produced images, including the corruption/auto-repair path) exists to build on.
Negative: a corrupted Config Snapshot, Parity Block, or Function Table currently goes undetected — check() reports overall status based on Superblock alone.

Mitigation: explicitly documented as a scope cut in the engine's README, not a silent gap; extending check() to the other three structures (verify-only for Function Table/Meta Table, XOR-reconstruct for Config Snapshot) is described there as known future work.

adrs.title: I/O Engine — confirm() Write Path Bypasses the Full SMART Flush Pipeline
adrs.context: ADR-002 defines the full crash-safe SMART flush order: V-SMART -> Cache SMART -> B-SMART -> WAL -> M-SMART, coordinated by the SMART Handler (ADR-001) and reconciled via smart_handler.py. That pipeline depends on the C-process architecture and IPC protocol, both still open per the project roadmap. The I/O Engine's confirm() stage needs to mark a mount as active (Superblock last_mount_time, SMART mount_count/clean_unmount_flag) today, independent of when that fuller pipeline gets built.
adrs.decision: confirm() writes last_mount_time directly to the Superblock, and — best-effort, if a usable M-SMART location was found at mount — increments mount_count and sets clean_unmount_flag = 0 directly on M-SMART. It does not go through V-SMART, Cache SMART, B-SMART, or the WAL.
rationale: Decoupling: the I/O Engine's own mount lifecycle shouldn't block on the SMART Handler pipeline's unresolved architecture questions.
Narrow, well-defined write: two fields, one direct write, no batching/reconciliation semantics to get wrong before the fuller pipeline exists.

Best-effort, not silent: a missing or unreadable M-SMART table doesn't fail confirm() — the Superblock write (the one thing every subsequent mount depends on) is what's fatal; the SMART write is a bonus that degrades gracefully.
consequences: Positive: confirm() is fully testable today without any dependency on ADR-001/002's pipeline being built.

Negative: this is a genuine bypass of ADR-002's stated flush order — mount_count/clean_unmount_flag updates from confirm() never touch Cache SMART, B-SMART, or the WAL, so they're not covered by that ADR's crash-recovery guarantees.

Mitigation: only two fields are affected, both low-cost to lose on crash (a missed mount_count increment is a lost counter tick, not corrupted data); B-SMART is not updated by confirm() either, so M-SMART/B-SMART can drift on these two fields specifically until the full pipeline lands — flagged in the engine's README, to be resolved when ADR-001/002's architecture is actually implemented.

adrs.title: I/O Engine — Language and Toolchain: Assembly + C, Not Rust, for V1
adrs.context: Two toolchains were on the table for the I/O Engine: (1) hand-written x86-64 assembly for the raw device syscalls plus C for everything else, or (2) Rust, for its compile-time memory-safety guarantees. A survey of existing Rust I/O crates (rio, safer-ring, io-engine, lio, and the foundational io-uring) was done specifically to check whether an existing, mature crate could shortcut this decision.
adrs.decision: V1 stays Assembly (raw syscalls: openat, pread64, pwrite64, fdatasync, close, ioctl) + C, matching the repo-wide BSD-3-Clause license. Rust remains under consideration for a future version, not adopted now.
rationale: Crate survey didn't find a clear win: rio is GPL-3.0 by default (MIT/Apache-2.0 only via paid GitHub Sponsors) — incompatible with BSD-3-Clause without paying for the exception. safer-ring is v0.0.1, 362 all-time downloads, single-maintainer — essentially unproven. io-engine and lio are legitimate and permissively licensed but small; neither removes enough risk to justify a mid-flight language switch.

Memory safety and specification correctness are different axes: Rust's compile-time guarantees rule out a category of bugs (use-after-free, data races) but do nothing to catch a wrong byte offset, wrong checksum algorithm, or misread field width against fs.info — the actual source of every bug found while building this engine (e.g. the O_DIRECT/_GNU_SOURCE CI-lint mismatch, the pointer_checksum_algo_used field that was declared but never populated) was specification/logic, not memory safety. A rewrite wouldn't have prevented either.

Working, tested code already exists: the C+asm engine passes 24/24 assertions against a real image (mkfs_cafs -> mount -> check -> remount -> confirm, plus corruption/auto-repair), including from a from-scratch checkout. Restarting in Rust discards that.
consequences: Positive: no license entanglement; matches the existing BSD-3-Clause repo without exception beyond the already-disclosed vendored BLAKE3.
Negative: forgoes Rust's memory-safety guarantees for this component — a real, non-zero cost for hand-written syscall wrappers and manual buffer arithmetic.

Mitigation: kept narrow in scope (six syscall wrappers, no complex ownership patterns) and covered by a real test suite exercised on every change; revisit if a Rust I/O crate matures (permissive license, real adoption, security audit) or if this component's complexity grows enough that manual memory management risk outweighs the switching cost.
Superseded: ADR-011 reversed this decision one day later on 2026-09-03, after re-evaluating against a different, more applicable category of Rust crates.

adrs.title: I/O Engine — Resolved fs.info Ambiguities for V1
adrs.context: Building the I/O Engine against fs.info surfaced several places where the spec doesn't fully define behavior needed for a working implementation: no stated addressing unit for "LBA," an invalid hex literal for the pointer-block magic, no stated bootstrap procedure for discovering the pointer-block checksum algorithm before anything has been verified yet, and an inconsistent use of "LBA" to mean two different things in different fields.
adrs.decision: Four resolutions, all implemented in cafs_io_layout.h and cited there: (1) LBA addressing unit: raw byte offset from device start, applied uniformly to real_lba/fallback_real_lba fields too. (2) Pointer block magic (fs.info writes 0xCAFSPTR, not valid hex — P/T/R aren't hex digits): the literal 8-byte ASCII string "CAFSPTR\0", compared byte-for-byte rather than parsed as an integer. (3) Pointer-block checksum algorithm bootstrap: try CRC32C, then XXHASH32, accept whichever matches. Both are the only two legal IDs per Sec.3.3; a false match between two different 4-byte algorithms on corrupted data is not a realistic risk. (4) function_table_anchor_lba = 4: this field holds the anchor slot index (0-5), not a byte offset — inconsistent with every other real_lba-style field in the format, which are byte offsets. mkfs_cafs writes literal 4; nothing currently reads it back to cross-check, consistent with the Superblock-only check policy (ADR-007).
rationale: Each of these blocks a specific, concrete piece of code (anchor offset math, magic comparison, first-ever checksum verification, Superblock field layout) — a decision had to be made one way or another to write anything at all. Recorded here rather than left as an undocumented implementation detail, so a fuller spec pass on fs.info can confirm or override each one deliberately.
consequences: Positive: unblocks implementation without waiting on a full spec revision; each choice is narrow and independently reversible.
Negative: fs.info itself remains unfixed — a future reader of fs.info alone (without this ADR) will still hit the same ambiguities.
Mitigation: fs.info should get a follow-up pass incorporating these four resolutions directly, closing this ADR out as "merged into the spec" rather than leaving it as a permanent patch on top.

adrs.title: I/O Engine — Rewritten in Rust, Superseding ADR-009
adrs.context: ADR-009 evaluated Rust I/O crates against the wrong workload category — io_uring wrappers (rio, safer-ring), suited to high-throughput async I/O, not CAFS V1's synchronous, low-frequency mount lifecycle. Re-evaluated against the right category (safe synchronous syscall wrappers: rustix, nix) and the mature, official checksum crates now available (blake3, crc32c, xxhash-rust), the calculus changed enough to warrant a full rewrite rather than a going-forward-only policy.
adrs.decision: The I/O Engine is rewritten in Rust. The C+asm version is retired — its files should be deleted from Src/FUSE/Linux/x86-64/I-O_Engine/, along with the now-unnecessary vendor/blake3/ (BLAKE3 is a normal Cargo dependency now, nothing is vendored).
rationale: Right-category crate survey found real, mature, permissively-licensed options where the wrong-category survey hadn't: rustix (985M downloads, MIT/Apache-2.0/Apache-2.0-with-LLVM-exception) and the official blake3/crc32c/xxhash-rust crates, versus rio's GPL-3.0 default license and safer-ring's v0.0.1 immaturity.

Concrete upgrades, not just a language change: blake3 brings automatic SIMD (the C engine was deliberately software-only); crc32c brings hardware acceleration via SSE4.2 (same C limitation fixed); OwnedFd's Drop closes the file descriptor automatically — no leak even if a caller forgets to call close(), unlike the C version.

A genuine, demonstrated compiler catch during the port: the first compile attempt rejected simultaneous immutable (whole-ctx, for the fd) and mutable (ctx.superblock) borrows in mount() — an aliasing mistake the C version had no equivalent guard against. Real evidence for the stated thesis (Rust catches a category of bugs C doesn't), not just an assertion.

Equally real evidence for the thesis's limit: while porting check(), the pointer-checksum-algorithm-used value was computed, assigned to a local, and never wired into the result struct — compiled clean, no warning, because it's a logic gap, not a type or borrow error. Only the integration test caught it. This is the same bug class found in the C version's pointer_checksum_algo_used field during that engine's own testing. Direct, repeated evidence that compile-time guarantees and specification/logic correctness are different axes — the switch reduces one category of risk, not all of it, and testing remains load-bearing either way.

Newtype safety, used concretely: ByteOffset is a distinct type from a bare u64, specifically to make ADR-010's documented gap (an anchor slot index and a byte offset being interchangeable uint64_t's in the C version, function_table_anchor_lba holding the former while every sibling field holds the latter) a compile error if reintroduced, not a silent bug waiting to happen again.
consequences: Positive: hardware-accelerated checksums, RAII fd management, a newtype that closes off a specific, already-documented bug class, and a test suite ported test-for-test (24 assertions worth of coverage preserved, not narrowed) confirming behavioral parity with the retired C version.
Negative: discards a working, tested C+asm implementation; the syscall layer's unsafe surface isn't zero (one ioctl, BLKGETSIZE64, needs it — see ADR-012) — memory safety is improved, not absolute.

Negative: local verification during this rewrite required pinning blake3/tempfile to older versions, because the sandbox's only available rustc (1.75.0, via apt) predates several transitive dependencies' move to the edition2024 Cargo feature. Not a defect in the decision — a normal toolchain (rustup, or this repo's own CI via dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable) doesn't hit it — but worth recording as an MSRV consideration for anyone building this outside CI on an older distribution's packaged Rust.

Mitigation: the C version's git history (if committed before deletion) remains the reference for behavioral parity; the integration test suite is the actual contract going forward, ported alongside the rewrite specifically so parity is checked, not assumed.

adrs.title: I/O Engine — Syscall Foundation: rustix
adrs.context: ADR-011 committed to Rust; a concrete syscall foundation still had to be picked between the two mature safe options found — rustix and nix — rather than an arbitrary choice made mid-rewrite.
adrs.decision: rustix, for all device I/O (open, pread/pwrite, fdatasync, and the one custom ioctl BLKGETSIZE64 needs).
rationale: Architectural alignment with the project's own stated syscall philosophy: rustix's own documentation describes doing direct syscalls via the asm! macro on supported platforms, bypassing libc entirely by default — the same "the kernel syscall is assembly" ethos the retired C engine's hand-written wrappers were built around, now safely wrapped and maintained by the Bytecode Alliance instead of hand-rolled.

Directly comparable real-world precedent: libblkio (a VIRTIO block-I/O library — a block-device-facing systems project of the same shape as this engine) migrated from nix to rustix specifically to simplify licensing. Not a generic popularity signal; a project solving a closely related problem made the same choice for a reason that transfers directly.
I/O-safety typestate: rustix is built around OwnedFd/AsFd, which is what makes CafsCtx::close()'s RAII fd-closing behavior (ADR-011) straightforward rather than something bolted on.

Verified, not assumed, for the one gap in rustix's API: it has no named wrapper for BLKGETSIZE64 (only BLKSSZGET/BLKPBSZGET). Confirmed by reading rustix 1.1.4's actual source before committing to it, and by test-compiling and running the custom ioctl (via rustix's own generic Getter<OPCODE, Output> pattern) against both a real file and a symbolic non-block-device target, confirming it round-trips a real device's size correctly and fails with the semantically correct ENOTTY against something that isn't a block device.

nix remains a reasonable alternative, not a rejected option on technical grounds — MIT-only (simpler single license, where rustix is a triple: Apache-2.0, Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception, or MIT), 55M downloads/month, used in 20K+ crates, with its own ioctl_read! macro that would have generated an equally usable BLKGETSIZE64 wrapper (precedented in the btrfs-uapi crate). This decision is closer to a coin flip resolved by the libblkio precedent and asm-based syscall alignment than a case where nix had a real deficiency.
consequences: Positive: the engine's entire device-I/O path is now one consistent library, verified end-to-end (open, read, write, sync, and the one ioctl) rather than assumed to work from documentation alone.
Positive: unsafe is isolated to a single, documented block (the BLKGETSIZE64 ioctl) — everything else in the engine is safe Rust.

Negative: nix was not evaluated to the same depth (no equivalent test-compile against this project's actual ioctl need) — if rustix turns out to have a real gap later, that comparison hasn't actually been done yet, only reasoned about.

Mitigation: low switching cost if this needs revisiting — rustix's usage is confined to a handful of call sites (mount.rs, block_io.rs, remount.rs, confirm.rs), not spread throughout the codebase via a leaky abstraction.

adrs.title: Global Speed-Index Tables (Non-Critical, Function-Table-Referenced)
adrs.context: An early proposal ("Global Hash Table") conflated a fast existence-check structure with the dedup table. They're different things with different criticality: dedup is authoritative data (correctness-critical), while a fast lookup index is a performance optimization that the filesystem must survive losing.
adrs.decision: One non-critical table, living in a block the Function Table points to (hash_table_lba): a Hash Table, binary, purely existence-check ("does this hash exist?"), keyed by a content hash (whole-file or per-LBA, config-selectable, mutually exclusive — see amendment) with the shared cross-table identifier as its value. Filename and LBA-range/permission data, originally proposed as two further non-critical tables here, were folded into the Identifier Table instead (see amendment) since both are already keyed by the same identifier and gain nothing from being split out.
rationale: Separating existence-check from name/location+permission avoids the collision hazard a single mixed-key table would have (a content hash colliding in value with a valid LBA, for instance).

Placing the Hash Table under the Function Table (non-critical tier, per ADR-006) rather than the Meta/User Table (critical tier) is a deliberate criticality choice: losing it costs lookup speed, not correctness, provided the fallback path (walking the authoritative Dedup Table / Identifier Table directly) holds.
consequences: Positive: a fast path for the common case (dedup/CoW existence checks) without making the filesystem's correctness depend on that fast path being intact.
Negative: the slow-path fallback (walking critical structures directly) needs to actually be built and kept behaviorally equivalent to the fast path.

Amendment (2026-09-06 session): the original three-table design (Hash / Filename / LBA) is superseded. Filename and LBA+permission data move to a new Identifier Table entry in the Meta/User Pointer Table (critical tier — this is load-bearing namespace data, not a speed cache, and belongs alongside btree_root_lba). Only the Hash Table remains under the Function Table. The Hash Table is config-toggleable: off, whole-file-hash, or per-LBA-hash (mutually exclusive — LBA-hash mode's detection coverage is a strict superset of file-hash mode's, so there is no reason to run both). Hash width is 256-bit (32 bytes), unfolded — unlike the corruption checksum, a collision here is a correctness issue (two different files treated as identical), not a tolerable non-event, so it is never truncated. Disabling the Hash Table entirely costs only time-to-reclaim (duplicate data persists until the background dedup routine finds it); it was never load-bearing.
Reconfirmed invariant: the shared cross-table identifier must be inode-like — assigned once per logical file, stable across renames, shared across hardlinks, never derived from filename or content.

adrs.title: Two-Tier Deduplication — File-Level Primary, LBA-Level "CoW Extreme" Fallback
adrs.context: ADR-013 separated the non-critical speed-index table(s) from the real dedup mechanism. That real mechanism needed its own decision: where it lives, and how it actually decides what's shareable.
adrs.decision: The authoritative dedup table lives in the Meta/User Pointer Table (dedup_table_root_lba, critical tier): 8-byte hash + 8-byte location_id + 8-byte offset + 4-byte length + 4-byte refcount, entries with refcount > 1. Deduplication happens in two tiers: (1) File-level (primary): whole-file content hash. If two files match, they share underlying storage. (2) LBA-level "CoW Extreme" (fallback): when file-level content doesn't match, individual blocks/extents are still checked and shared at block granularity via a separate hash-of-LBA-contents structure, so two files that mostly differ but share some blocks still get partial storage savings.
rationale: Whole-file dedup is cheap to check and covers the common case (identical files) with one hash comparison.

Falling back to block-level matching only when whole-file matching fails avoids paying block-level hashing cost for every file, while still catching partial-overlap cases whole-file hashing would miss entirely.

Keeping the authoritative table in the critical tier (Meta/User Table) is consistent with ADR-013's separation: dedup refcounts are correctness-bearing (a wrong refcount means either premature space reclamation of still-referenced data, or a permanent leak) — this cannot be a table the filesystem shrugs off losing.
consequences: Positive: catches both the cheap common case and a meaningfully broader set of partial-match cases, at a cost proportional to how often the cheap case fails.

Negative: two hashing/lookup paths to build and keep correct instead of one; the block-level path's hash-of-LBA-contents structure needs its own consistency story (recomputed on every write to that LBA, or invalidated and lazily recomputed).

Negative: refcount correctness under concurrent writers is the same hard problem every CoW-with-dedup design has — not solved by this decision, just scoped to where it has to be solved (the critical-tier table, not the speed-index tables).

Open (2026-09-06 session): dedup hash collision insurance policy — verify newly-written data asynchronously (at FS block-size granularity, after mount, on first read/write) before a hash match is trusted enough to actually collapse two blocks into one shared copy; a background hash-daemon (started immediately at mount, normally low priority, schedulable at elevated/exclusive priority to catch up faster, with a supervised-process fallback per ADR-015 if it fails) builds/maintains the hash index. Data is always written safely first; sharing only happens after verification confirms the match.

adrs.title: Process Architecture — Master/mntproc as Separate Supervised Processes, Housekeeping as Separate Children
adrs.context: Researched against PostgreSQL's postmaster architecture (one coordinator, fixed background maintenance workers — checkpointer, background writer, WAL writer, autovacuum launcher — plus per-connection backends, all parent-child, all supervised). An earlier framing called the housekeeping tasks (defrag, balance, python/SMART) "coroutines" — corrected: they're dispatched as non-critical asynchronous tasks, important but not allowed to take the FUSE processor down if they fail. That correction settles the process-vs-thread question: a crashing thread can take its whole process with it; a crashing process is cleanly reaped by the kernel (SIGCHLD to the parent) with everything else untouched. The isolation this design needs only exists at the process boundary.
adrs.decision: Per mounted partition: one master process, parent of one mntproc (the FUSE request handler) and of one separate child process per housekeeping task (defrag, balance, python/SMART each their own child — not run inline inside master, mirroring how checkpointer/bgwriter/autovacuum-launcher are each separate from postmaster and from each other). Master supervises all of them. A housekeeping child's failure must not crash mntproc and must not force an fsck. Recovery from a housekeeping task's partial/failed work goes through the WAL's existing revert mechanism, not through filesystem-check.
rationale: Process, not thread, isolation is what "failure shouldn't bring the FS down" actually requires — this is why coroutines-as-threads-inside-master was corrected.
Per-task children, not one inline batch inside master, gets task-vs-task isolation for free in addition to task-vs-mntproc isolation: defrag crashing doesn't take balance down either.

fsck avoidance is the explicit design goal, not a side effect — an extra fsck after every housekeeping hiccup is "honestly not preferred by anyone." The WAL is the mechanism already present in the design (per fs.info's checksum-failure and recovery sections) capable of reverting partial damage without a full consistency scan, so housekeeping-task failure is scoped to be a WAL-revertible event, not an fsck-triggering one.
Supervision requires parent-child, per the Postgres precedent (ADR-016 covers the separate question of preventing more than one master per partition).
consequences: Positive: a housekeeping task can fail, restart, or be killed without affecting live FUSE I/O or requiring a filesystem-wide consistency check.

Negative: more processes to supervise than a thread-based design — master's supervision logic (detect a dead child, decide whether/how to restart it, decide when repeated failure means giving up and surfacing an error) is real code that has to exist and be correct, not a simplification deferred to "the OS handles it."

Negative: WAL-revertibility of housekeeping-task partial work is now a hard requirement, not an assumption — a housekeeping task whose partial state can't be cleanly reverted via WAL would violate this ADR's whole premise. Needs to be checked per task (defrag and balance both move data around; either could plausibly leave a state the WAL wasn't designed to revert if not built with this requirement in mind from the start).

adrs.title: Partition Singleton Locking — flock() Keyed by volume_uuid
adrs.context: An earlier proposal used "oldest process / lowest PID" to determine which process is master for a partition. Researched against PostgreSQL's actual mechanism: a data directory is protected by a lockfile (postmaster.pid), checked and validated at startup, with the OS's own advisory lock as a second line of defense against a stale file from a crashed instance — not PID comparison. PID-based election has two concrete failure modes on the intended target platform: PIDs get reused after wraparound, so "lowest PID" doesn't reliably mean "oldest" once the real oldest process exits; and under PID namespaces (any container runtime — Docker, Podman, systemd-nspawn), raw PID values aren't comparable across processes in different namespaces at all. Separately: no two partitions should ever handle each other's I/O — a cp/mv between two mounted volumes is not one partition reaching into another's data, the same way one NTFS volume never "handles" a second NTFS volume's partition.
adrs.decision: flock() on a lockfile keyed by the Superblock's volume_uuid — not by device path, not by mount point path, not by PID. Whoever holds the lock is master for that partition; the OS releases it automatically if the holder dies.
rationale: Structural guarantee, not enforced logic: only one process can hold an exclusive flock() on a given file at a time — "one master per partition" falls out of the locking primitive itself rather than needing separate election code to get right.

Automatic crash recovery: the OS drops the lock when the holding process dies, so a crashed master doesn't need a heartbeat/liveness protocol for another process to safely determine it's gone and take over.

volume_uuid, not device path: device paths shift under controller renumbering (/dev/sdb1 becoming /dev/sdc1 across a reboot is common) — locking on the device path could let a partition acquire two different locks across two device enumerations, or fail to recognize it's the same partition it already holds a lock for. volume_uuid is stable by construction (it's the Superblock's own identity field) and correctly answers "is this the same partition" regardless of what the OS currently calls the device.

Directly resolves the "partitions don't handle each other's I/O" requirement: distinct volume_uuids mean distinct lock paths, and a process only ever acquires the lock for the specific partition it's mounting — there's no shared namespace where one partition's master could accidentally acquire authority over another's.
consequences: Positive: no election protocol to design, implement, or get wrong; correct behavior under process crashes, container/namespace boundaries, and device renumbering, all as a consequence of using the right primitive rather than three separate fixes.

Negative: requires a well-known, stable filesystem location to place these lockfiles (e.g. /run/cafs/<volume_uuid>.lock) that's writable by whatever's attempting the mount — a small new operational dependency (that directory existing and being writable) that PID comparison didn't have.

Mitigation: this is a standard, well-understood Unix pattern (single-instance daemons have used lockfile-based mutual exclusion for decades) — not a novel mechanism being introduced, just the correct application of an existing one.

adrs.title: Allocator Mode Toggle — Balance / Performance / Safety, Independent Interfaces
adrs.context: The Allocator's process architecture (library-linked vs. its own process vs. merged with the I/O Engine) was left open pending research. That research suggested each option's cost centers on cross-process coordination for concurrent access to allocator state, and proposed resolving it with one interface designed to work identically whether calls are local (performance) or IPC-routed (safety) — so the transport could change without the protocol changing. That specific proposal was considered and rejected: forcing one interface shape across all three modes would have constrained performance mode to fit inside whatever safety mode's IPC-oriented protocol needs, which defeats the point of a performance mode existing at all.
adrs.decision: Three config-toggled modes — balance, performance, safety — each free to have its own interface if it needs one. Safety mode: sacrifices speed deliberately, uses IPC and multiple processes specifically so a single critical crash doesn't break the drive for anyone currently writing data, and specifically avoids ever needing fsck. Performance mode: gets to be genuinely fast — no protocol constraint inherited from safety mode's IPC design; gets its own interface if that's what speed requires. Balance mode: the next concrete build priority (ahead of both other modes' implementations). Mode-specific code lives in its own subfolder under Allocator/ (e.g. Allocator/Performance/), per the repo's shared-code-one-level-up convention applied recursively: shared allocator code sits at Allocator/, and each mode's divergent code sits one level below it.
rationale: Modularity over forced uniformity: the repo's own stated design principle ("everything is a folder," shared code one level above its consumers) already implies mode-specific divergence is expected and structurally accounted for — a forced single interface would have fought that principle rather than used it.

Safety mode's whole purpose is the crash/fsck guarantee, which specifically justifies its performance cost (IPC, multiple processes) — that cost has no reason to also apply to performance mode, which has a different, opposite purpose.

Balance-first sequencing is the sensible default to actually build against: it's the mode most users will run, and building it first gives performance and safety mode real code to diverge from rather than three parallel designs built independently with no shared baseline at all.
consequences: Positive: performance mode is not held back by safety mode's transport requirements; each mode can be evaluated and optimized on its own terms.

Negative: up to three allocator interfaces to maintain instead of one — a bug fix or behavior change discovered in one mode doesn't automatically apply to the others, and needs to be deliberately ported if it should.

Negative: no shared protocol means no "flip a config flag and the transport changes underneath the same calls" capability — switching a live system between modes (if that's ever wanted) is a heavier operation than a transport swap, closer to a reconfigure-and-restart.

Mitigation: balance mode being built first, with performance/safety as explicit divergences from it (living in their own subfolders, not parallel from-scratch trees), keeps the three from drifting into three unrelated implementations that happen to share a name.
